tagline.text: A 1 km white-sand beach and sunset rock pool at the western edge of Pangasinan in Burgos

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,100~3,500 (from Manila, per person for 2 days and 1 night)

children.text: Cabongaoan Beach is a white-sand beach about 1 km long in Burgos, at the western edge of Pangasinan. A popular 2-day, 1-night trip combines a sunset over the western sea from this quiet, little-developed beach with a walk to the "Death Pool" in the rocks at its northern end.

Cabongaoan Beach belongs to the municipality of Burgos, at the western edge of Pangasinan, which holds the westernmost point of Luzon. Wikipedia lists it as the main attraction of Burgos and describes a natural tidal pool that fills with water as waves crash against the rocks. The beach is about 1 km long and faces the West Philippine Sea (South China Sea). The sand ranges from white to cream, and rocks show along parts of the shoreline.

The appeal of this beach is that facilities are not crowded together as on famous resort beaches. Along the shore there are only a few small resorts and homestay-style lodgings, and almost no restaurants or shops. That suits you if you want to rest to the sound of the waves or pitch a tent and watch the stars, but it can be inconvenient if you expect amenities. It is also not particularly close to Manila, so an overnight stay is better than a day trip. Weekends in peak season can be crowded, so consider a weekday visit if quiet is your goal.

At the northern end of the beach, among limestone rocks and cliffs, is a natural pool known as the "Death Pool." It is known as a deep pool and gets its name from that reputation, and waves and tides can make it dangerous, so it is not a place to enter at any time. Think of it as a place to look at on foot, and go during a safe time after checking the tide and waves.
Transport is the biggest variable on this trip. You take a bus from Manila to Alaminos, then a tricycle from Burgos town for another
1 hour
or so, and there are almost no tricycles in the beach village. The knack for this trip is to arrange your ride back in advance.

White to cream sand stretches long toward the western sea. It is not crowded, so it is good for walking, and since rocks show at the water's edge in places, it is best to decide on a swimming area first.
The beach faces west, so you can watch the sun go down from anywhere along it. The easiest way is to wait for the glow at a table at a resort right on the beach or on the sand.

blocks.title: Rock walk to the Death Pool

children.text: Walk along the rocks from the north end of the beach and you reach a natural pool among limestone cliffs. Many visitors say it takes about
10–20 minutes
on foot, and the rocks are sharp, so sturdy footwear is essential.
You can rent a tent spot at a resort and spend the night close to the sand. If you want shade and a toilet, bring a hammock and tent and book ahead.
Burgos is a quiet rural area of rolling hills with free-roaming cattle ranches. On the way to the beach you see village life, fields and the sea together.

blocks.title: Day trip to Colibra Island and Tambobong Beach

children.text: You can hire a bangka from your lodging for a boat tour to Colibra Island, Tambobong Beach and other places. The schedule changes with waves and tides, so ask your lodging about that day's conditions.
Take a night bus from Pasay or Cubao in Manila to Alaminos. If you go by daytime bus, leave early in the morning so you arrive before dark.
After arriving in Alaminos, have a light breakfast and transfer to a bus bound for Santa Cruz (Zambales). Get off at the Burgos public market.
At the Burgos public market, stock up on water, snacks and lunch. There are almost no restaurants at the beach, so you need to buy now.
Take a tricycle to Cabongaoan. Get the driver's contact number for the ride back.
Check in at your resort, have lunch, then swim inside the safety lines.
If the tide and waves look safe, walk north along the beach to the Death Pool and back.
Return to the beach for the sunset. Eat dinner at the resort or have the food you brought.
On the second day, you usually stroll the beach in the morning and check out around
. If you reach Burgos town around lunchtime and return to Manila via Alaminos, you arrive late in the evening.
Set out from Alaminos, pass through Burgos and continue to the beach.
Arrive, rent a table or open cottage and enjoy a swim.
Check the tide and waves and look at the Death Pool.
Watch the sunset and head back to town before dark.
The village roads are narrow and there is almost no light at night. It is safer to get back to the main road before dark.

From the Burgos public market, take a tricycle to the beach. It is about 4–5 km, with unpaved and narrow stretches, and takes about
30 minutes–1 hour
. Reported fares are
(for 2–4 people), and you can haggle, but it is hard to go below the rate locals pay.
Most reports say there is no direct bus from Manila to Burgos. Bus schedules and fares change, so check the latest information at the terminal.
It is about
270 km
from Manila to Burgos. The usual route takes expressways, passes Alaminos in western Pangasinan and continues toward Burgos. It takes roughly
5–7 hours
; check tolls locally.
The road from town to the beach is narrow and rough, and gas stations are scarce. Fill your tank before you set out. Some reports mention a vehicle parking fee of about
on the beach side.

items.title: The last stretch to the beach

There are almost no tricycles in the beach village, so the surest way is to set your return time and ask a driver in advance to pick you up.

Western Pangasinan has good weather in the dry season, which suits swimming and sunset watching. November to May is a good time to travel, and lodging fills early on weekends and in the April–May peak season.

In the rainy season the waves get higher, the area around the Death Pool becomes dangerous and the road turns muddy. If a typhoon is forecast, postpone your trip. During the day, morning and mid-afternoon are good for avoiding the midday sun, and the sunset can be seen from anywhere on the beach.

Along the beach there are small resorts and homestays. Names that come up often in reports include Roven's Place, Amayaj Bora Beach Resort, Villa Toledo and Cabo Resort, and D'Cousins Beach Resort. Rooms range from fan rooms to air-conditioned rooms, cottages and tent spots. Operating status and rates change, so be sure to contact them first and book. They fill early on weekends and in peak season.

There are almost no restaurants at the beach. Some resorts take orders from a limited menu or offer cooking service, and drinks are on sale, but the surest way to eat is to shop at the Burgos town market and bring food. Some reports mention rules against eating on the beach or near the water, so follow your lodging's instructions.

If you like instant food such as ramen, instant rice and cup meals, you can bring them with a burner and cook with your lodging's permission. Cooking and eating rules differ by lodging, so ask when you book.
If you travel from Manila, a night bus that reaches Alaminos at dawn is the way to make the most of the day.
Get your return tricycle driver's contact number when you arrive. There are almost no tricycles in the beach village.
Buy food and drinking water in advance at the Burgos public market. There are almost no shops at the beach.
Phone signal is unstable. Download maps beforehand and set meeting times.
For the Death Pool, there are many sharp rocks, so aqua shoes or sturdy sandals are a must.
Check the tide table and go at low tide, which is safer.
On weekends and in April–May, book lodging ahead and check the checkout time.
Bring plenty of cash. In a remote village, some places may not accept cards or e-payments, so check with your lodging beforehand.
On hot days wear sandals on the sand, and bring sunscreen and a hat. Many stretches have little shade.
Carry your trash out and keep the beach clean. In a remote village, garbage collection is difficult.
Around the Death Pool, waves and tides can suddenly become strong and dangerous. Do not go near when waves are high or the tide is coming in.
Do not swim beyond the safety lines set by the local government unit (LGU). There are reports that currents between the rocks are dangerous.
Sharp rocks can cut your feet, so do not walk barefoot across the rocky area.
It is better not to take children toward the Death Pool because of the cliffs and rough rocks.
There is almost no light on the roads at night, so finish moving around before dark.
Fees, rules and operating status change, so check the latest announcements with your lodging and the Burgos municipal tourism contact.
A rock pool about
10–20 minutes
on foot from the north end of the beach. Look at it only when the tide and waves are safe.
A small island about
45 minutes
by bangka from the beach. Some reports say there is little to do there besides swimming.
A beach in neighboring Dasol. It is sometimes combined by lodging boat tours or tricycle; check the schedule locally.
